source_text: ᾿Ἐξαιτοῦμαι δὲ παρά τε φιλοσόφων τῶν νῦν ὄντων, σοὺυς αὐτὸς ἔγνων καὶ ὃσους ἄλλων διηγουμένων ἤκουσα, καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων, ἀνεμεσήτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ νῦν ἡμῖν λεγόμενα. μηδέ μέ τις ἢ φιλίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα ἢ καὶ ἀπτεχϑανόμενον ἔτι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις (ὧν, εἴπτερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐραστής ve διὰ τοὺς λόγους εἶναι ϑέλω, καὶ εὐφημεῖν αὐτοὺς βούλομαι αὐτός τε καὶ ἑτέρων τὰ κάλλιστα λεγόντων περὶ αὐτῶν ἀκούεξιν᾽ ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτά ἐστιν, ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον περιϊβρίζεσϑαι μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων σχεδὸν καὶ τοὔνομα τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἐμὲ δὲ μικροῦ δεῖν ἰδιωτεύειν ἑλέσϑαι πτάντη, ἤπερ τι μαϑεῖν ὧν οὗτοι ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, οἷς διὰ τὸν λοιττὸν βίον οὐδὲ προσιέναι ἄξιον εἶναι ἐδόκουν, ἴσως οὐκ ὀρϑῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν), πλὴν μή μέ τις φιλοτιμίᾳ τινὶ ἤτοι τῶν εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἐπαίνων ἢ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω φιλοσόφους ἄλλῃ ταύτῃ φιλο- τὸ τιμίᾳ ταῦτα λέγειν ὑπονοησάτω" ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρότερα ἡμᾶς τῶν αὐτοῖ: ἔργων, μὴ κολακεύειν δοχοίημεν, λέγειν τεεττείσϑω οὐχὲ ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐντέχνους ἐγχωμίων ἑαυτοῖς ἐχποριζομένοις" ὃς οὐδ᾽ ὕτε μειράκιον ὧν τὴν δημώδη ῥητορικὴν ἔχ. ῥήτορος ἐδιδασκόμην, ἐπαινεῖν καὶ τὸ λέγειν περί του ἐγκώμιον, ὃ τι μὴ ἀληϑὲς ἦν, ἑκὼν ὑπέμενον. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ νῦν ἐπαινεῖν ττροϑέμενος, ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἑτέρων ψόγοις τοῦτον ἐξαίρειν οἶμαι δεῖν" ἢ κακῶς ἂν ἔλεγον τὸν ἄνδρα, τοῖς ἄλλων πταίσμασιν, ἵνα τι ττερὶ αὐτοῦ μεῖζον δὴ λέγειν ἔχοιμι, τταραβαλὼν τὸν μακάριον αὐτοῦ βίον" οὐχ οὕτως ἀφραίνομεν᾽ ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸ ὃ πέπονθα δίχα τινὸς παραβολῆς χαὶ τεανουργίας τῆς ἐν λόγοις ὁμολογήσω.
pass_a_gloss: But I demand from both the philosophers who are now and whom I myself knew and as many as I heard from others telling, and from the other people, to have without partiality towards the things now being said to us. Let no one either because of friendship towards the man or even still being dependent on the other philosophers (whom, if someone else, and I myself being a lover of words wish to be and I want to speak well of them, and I hear others speaking the best things about them) but for these are such that they are being utterly despised by almost everyone and the name of philosophy, I am about to choose to be a private person rather than to learn anything of what these announce, to whom because of the rest of their life it did not seem worthy to approach), except let no one suppose that I say these things because of some ambition either of the praises towards the man or of the other ambition towards the external philosophers. But also let us not seem to flatter, saying lesser things than their deeds, and let us not say words and names and clever expressions, which they themselves invent for themselves. For I was not even taught as a young man the common rhetoric of a rhetorician, to praise and to say an encomium about something which was not true, I endured willingly. Therefore, not even now, being about to praise, do I think it necessary to extol him simply by the censures of others, or to speak badly of the man because of the faults of others, so that I might have something greater to say about him, having disparaged the blessed life of him. We do not think in this way; but I will acknowledge what I have experienced, without any comparison and cleverness in words.
pass_b_english: I ask this of the philosophers now living—those I knew myself and those I heard about from others—and of everyone else: receive what I am about to say without bias. Let no one assume I speak from friendship toward the man, or because I still cling to the other philosophers (whom, if anyone else does, I myself—being a lover of the word—wish to honor, and I want to speak well of them and hear others speak well of them). But these philosophers are so utterly despised by almost everyone that the very name of philosophy is scorned; I would rather choose a private life than learn anything from men who, because of their conduct, seemed unworthy even to approach—though I may have judged that wrongly. Still, let no one suppose I say this from some ambition, whether from praise for the man or from rivalry toward outside philosophers. Nor let us appear to flatter by saying less than their deeds deserve, nor let us offer up words, names, and crafted phrases that they themselves invent for self-praise. For even as a youth I was not taught the common rhetoric of the rhetorician—to praise and deliver an encomium for something untrue—and I willingly endured that lack. So now, when I am about to praise, I do not think it right to exalt him merely by censuring others, or to speak ill of the man because of others' faults so that I might have something greater to say about him, disparaging his blessed life. That is not how we think; rather, I will simply acknowledge what I have experienced, without comparison or verbal artifice.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex syntax of the Greek, particularly the parenthetical remarks regarding the author's attitude toward other philosophers and his own rhetorical training. Pass B correctly interprets the conditional/parenthetical 'ἴσως οὐκ ὀρθῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν' (though I may have judged that wrongly) which Pass A rendered more loosely. The distinction between 'words' (λόγους) and 'clever expressions' (ἐντέχνους) is maintained.

The Greek text is correctly identified as Gregory Thaumaturgus' Panegyric to Origen, and the translation accurately reflects the source. The title 'Against Mere Word-Sages' appropriately captures the thought of the passage. The translation preserves the meaning, including the nuances of agency, negation, and modality. Scripture citations are not present in this passage, so no issues arise there. The translation is faithful to the source text, and no errors or omissions are found.
